newsitem.title: CHINA: China yuan market seen volatile on debt control.
newsitem.headline: China yuan market seen volatile on debt control.

text.p: China's recent move to ban state banks from trading on the state debt repurchase market will cause short-term volatility in interest rates and turnover on the domestic local currency market, analysts said on Thursday.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, last week decided to ban all state banks from trading on the nation's state debt repo market to try to stop banks from speculating on China's fledgling stock markets, traders said.
The ban is to take effect gradually and the central bank has not yet set a deadline in order to give the state banks time to offset their existing positions, they said.
"More and more bank money is flowing into the interbank market from the repo market," said one interbank market trader.
"With no deadline having been set, irregular money inflows will cause interest rates to move in a wider range and daily (interbank) turnover to fluctuate sharply in the short term," the trader said.

The ban followed a similar move in February prohibiting the four major state banks -- the Industrial and Commercial Bank, the Construction Bank, the Agricultural Bank, and the Bank of China -- from trading on the repo market.

Traders said those banks have already withdrawn from the market, which was launched in early 1996 to allow banks and other financial institutions to move short-term money amongst each other in periods of up to 120 days.
Trading volume on the interbank market hit 59.889 billion yuan ($7.22 billion) in May, with daily volume averaging 2.852 billion yuan, a surge of 42.73 percent from April, exchange statistics show.
The head offices of major state banks traded actively in May, with money borrowed and lent rocketing 171.29 percent and 67.72 percent respectively, the figures show.
Analysts said the state debt ban was in line with Beijing's efforts to expand the interbank market and would benefit China's financial system in the long run.

"Despite a rise in turnover in recent weeks, volume on the market is still far short of meeting the goal of making the market a barometer of short-term money movements in China," said one banker. "Potential for the market's expansion is great."

On Wednesday, turnover on the market hit a 1997 high of 6.9 billion yuan, but that figure is still far below the average 10 billion yuan daily turnover on each of the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges.
"The repo market has many irregularities," another banker said.
"Forcing more bank money into the more standardised interbank market will benefit China's financial markets in the long run," he said.
The interbank market is divided into two trading tiers.

Headquarters of 20 major state banks and 35 big short-term financial centres, or money brokerages run by the central bank, are first-tier trading members and can trade directly through the exchange's computerised system.

Branches of major banks, small banks and other domestic financial institutions including securities houses, plus a number of designated foreign banks, are second-tier members who can only trade through the short-term financial centres.
Analysts said one key reason for the light volume on the market was the limited number of first-tier trading members.

The central government has said it intends to drastically expand the interbank market this year and analysts expect one of the measures will be to allow hundreds of urban cooperative banks to take part in first-tier trading.
